extracted.intended_audience: the higher and middle classes (explicitly addressed in the sermon)
extracted.subtask_short: lay sermon to higher and middle classes
extracted.subtask_description: A public moral and political address diagnosing causes of social distress after peace, criticizing demagogues and social tendencies, and prescribing cultural antidotes (philosophy, religion, rank) to commercial excess. It aims to persuade civic elites and middle classes to adopt temperate judgments and revive intellectual/religious counter-forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish immediate occasions from true causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate occasions of existing distress must be distinguished from its true seat and sources; the former may be obvious historic facts, but the latter require deeper analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists on resolving the problem into underlying causes (e.g., overbalance of the commercial spirit and lack of counter-weights) rather than attributing everything to a single public event such as peace. 'The immediate occasions of the existing distress may be directly given with no greater difficulty... but toward the discovery of its true seat and sources I can but offer a humble contribution.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing distress to removable, personal causes (beware demagogues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let popular grief be transformed into grievance targeted at individuals or whole classes by incendiaries; false attributions to removable causes fuel sedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that when suffering is to 'supply air and fuel to their passions' it must be attributed to causes represented as removable. Demagogues exploit 'the needy' with 'lying words.' Remedy: administer the truth beforehand; show that the alleged causes cannot be easily removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple arithmetic and common sense to test popular claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Test sweeping popular assertions (e.g., that pensions or sinecures cause widespread distress) by simple, elementary arithmetic and cooler reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in text: the claim that the low wages of a man arise because sums are paid as annuities rather than to others is shown to be implausible by the 'first and simplest rules of arithmetic.' The audience is urged to 'stand out against the simple question' in a cooler mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and counterbalance the overbalance of the commercial spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: An excess attachment to temporal and personal objects (commercialism) must be counteracted by permanent intellectual and moral pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author identifies the main cause of exigencies as an 'overbalance in the commercial spirit in consequence of the absence or weakness of the counter-weights.' He prescribes fostering those counter-forces to rebalance society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revive the ancient feeling of rank and ancestry as a counter-force
rubrics_metrics.description: A cultivated sense of rank and ancestry historically served as a restraint on greed and appropriation, and its decline removes one check on the pursuit of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text acknowledges both good and evil in this feeling but treats it as a 'counterpoise to the grosser superstition for wealth.' It recommends reappreciating its restraining influence while noting possible attendant evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote philosophy and a learned public to moderate pursuit of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a serious philosophic class and a philosophic public disciplines minds toward permanent truths and counteracts the appetite for immediate profit and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author blames the 'general neglect of all the austere studies; the long and ominous eclipse of philosophy' for weakening society's counterforces. He argues that the 'pursuit of truth for its own sake' calms and counteracts the pursuit of wealth, and laments the usurpation of philosophy's name by empiricism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage mere dilettantism and amateur distraction as inadequate counterweights
rubrics_metrics.description: Amateur pursuits (dilettanti hobbies) are harmless in themselves but insufficient as counter-forces to commercialism when they replace serious philosophic or religious engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes between ingenuous pursuits (music, botany, antiquarianism) and the missing 'counterpoise': these amusements cannot substitute for the discipline of serious studies that regulate desires and temper wealth-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist that religion must engage intellect and affections to be an effective moral force
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion ought to be a full, intellectual, and affectionate engagement with eternal truths; mere acquiescence, ritual, or 'plain' faith without study is insufficient to restrain passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon specifies a sincere Christianity 'which demands the first-fruits of the whole man, his affections no less than his outward acts, his understanding equally with his feelings.' It critiques forms of faith that are 'acquiescence without insight' and urges study (Paul's admonitions are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the notion that Christianity is merely plain and requires no study
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissing Christianity as a few plain doctrines that need no deeper study is a misconception that weakens faith and public moral energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises Socinians/Unitarians who claim 'plainness and simplicity' and shows that scriptural writings contain depths requiring continual study. He references St. Paul and the necessity of adding 'knowledge' to faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deepen faith by ongoing intellectual study: the more profound the truth the simpler it becomes
rubrics_metrics.description: True religious and philosophical truth benefits from continual study; profundity ultimately yields simplicity but requires intellectual enlargement to sustain heartfelt faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: 'All truth indeed is simple, and needs no extrinsic ornament. And the more profound the truth is, the more simple.' The sermon stresses that the 'energies of the intellect, increase of insight, and enlarging views' keep faith alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm public passions by demonstrating inability of elites to have prevented economic shocks
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce public anger, show convincingly that those above were not able to prevent the hardship; conviction that blame is misplaced calms bitterness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes: 'nothing calms the mind in the hour of bitterness so efficaciously as the conviction that it was not within the means of those above us... to have prevented it.' Thus public explanation should emphasise limitations of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of incendiary rhetoric and slanderous tongues in public meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Public meetings are fertile ground for bold assertions and slander; such rhetoric magnifies grievances and may lead to unrest and violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon warns that 'a slanderous tongue has disquieted many' and demagogues 'would snatch the last morsel from the poor man's lips to make him curse the government.' It prescribes resisting such rhetoric and exposing false claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reasoned demonstration over assertion when addressing national economic issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments about public finance and causes of distress should rely on reasoned demonstration, arithmetic, and sound evidence rather than invective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the text the author rebukes rash popular attributions (e.g., blaming annuities/pensions) and insists on cooler mood, demonstrative argument, and 'mathematical demonstration' where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the historic credibility and doctrinal claims: require competent witnesses and honest interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: When appealing to historic events (e.g., Resurrection) as foundations for doctrine, rely on the accuracy and competence of the original biographers and avoid facile reinterpretation that strips events of their doctrinal force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon argues that historic credibility depends on the 'accuracy and competence of the writers who first recorded His acts and sayings,' and criticizes modern attempts to reduce miraculous events to mere moral examples.
